## Today is different {.center}

No slides to lecture from. No demo.

. . .

A **critique**: we look at each other's work and ask better questions about it.

## Work as inquiry, not delivery {.smaller}

Most classes: you hand in a finished thing, it gets a grade.

. . .

Today: your work is treated as a **question in progress**.

- not "is it done?"
- but "what is it *asking*?"

. . .

That's how artists and researchers actually talk about work.

## What you brought {.smaller}

Each person shares **two things**:

1. One piece of semester work that sits in **uncertainty** —
   something you're not sure *worked*, or not sure *what it means*
2. One **open question** the work raises —
   phrased so it can't be answered with yes/no

## Critique norms {.smaller}

- **Describe before you judge** — say what you actually see/read/hear first
- **Questions over verdicts** — "what happens if…" beats "I liked / didn't like"
- **The maker listens first** — don't defend; take notes, respond at the end
- **Be specific** — "the second room" not "the vibe"

# Critique rounds {background-color="#003da5"}

Small groups, then full class

## Round structure

Per person *(scale to group size)*:

- **2 min** — maker shares the work + the open question
- **3 min** — group responds: describe, then wonder aloud
- **1 min** — maker responds: what landed, what they'll try

. . .

Rotate. Everyone shares once.

## Discussion anchors {.smaller}

Pull one in when a critique stalls:

- **"Using" vs "making with"** — was the tool an instrument, or a collaborator you argued with?
- **Authorship** — when a system generated part of it, whose work is it?
- **Local vs service** — would running it on your own machine change what the piece *means*?

## Exercise — one question, not one answer {background-color="#ffb81c"}

*Individual · 5 min, then share*

Write the single **open question** your semester work generates.

. . .

Test it: if someone could answer it in one sentence, it's too small. Rewrite.

# Final Project {background-color="#003da5"}

Kickoff · planning starts now

## The one requirement

Your Final Project must **combine at least two competencies** from Weeks 1–8.

. . .

Not two tools used side by side — two that **need each other** for the piece to work.

## The competency menu {.smaller}

| Week | You can now… |
|---|---|
| 1 · Design & Textiles | design and fabricate soft/physical objects |
| 2 · Circuits & Animatronics | wire sensors and actuators to behavior |
| 3 · 3D Printing | model and print physical parts |
| 4 · Animation & VFX | build motion and composited image |
| 5 · Writing as Code | branching + generative text systems |
| 6 · Creative Code | generative visuals (p5.js), game-space (Bitsy) |
| 7 · Machine Learning | train / deploy a model as creative material |
| 8 · Local AI | run and interrogate a model you control |

## Example combinations

- **Gesture control + ML** — PoseNet drives a physical animatronic
- **Interactive fiction + generative graphics** — Twine branches that render p5.js scenes
- **Physical + digital** — a 3D-printed object that speaks lines from a local LLM
- **Textiles + circuits** — a wearable that responds to a sensor

## Exercise — project one-liner {background-color="#ffb81c"}

*Individual · 10 min*

Write:

1. Your project **in one sentence**
2. The **two competencies** it combines — and why it needs both
3. The **first file or part** you'll make

## Pair and pitch

*Pairs · 10 min*

Pitch your one-liner. Your partner asks:

- Which competency is doing the **heavy lifting**?
- What's the **smallest version** you could build first?

## What to bring to Week 9

- An **idea** you can say out loud
- **Started files** — a sketch, a doc, a wired breadboard, *something*

. . .

Week 9 is a work session, not a start-from-zero session.

## Assignment recap — Week 8

- **Local AI Log** — 5 experimental questions answered
- **Three-prompt exercise** — local vs cloud, compared
- **A creative artifact** — text, conversation export, or HTML page
- **`reflection.md`** — ~300 words, 5 sections

## Reflection prompt

> What changes when you run an AI on your own computer vs. accessing one through a browser? Who controls the tool — and does that change how you use it or trust it?

Consider: privacy · connectivity · speed · model size · who sets the content rules.

## The whole seminar, one line {.center}

You learned to **make with** these tools

by understanding **how they're built**.

. . .

That's the difference between a user and a maker.
